source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 1 (PDF 1-21, printed 1-21); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 1 (Periodic Table and Periodic Properties), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The periodic table of elements is rightly referred to as the:
blocks.explanation: The chapter calls the periodic table the "Symbol of Chemistry", a vital source of chemical knowledge (1.1).

book_ref.quote: refer to the periodic table of elements as the

blocks.prompt: 2 The modern periodic table provides the foundation for understanding how many elements?
blocks.explanation: The current table is the foundation for comprehending 118 elements and their properties (1.1).

book_ref.quote: It provides the foundation for comprehending 118 elements and their properties

blocks.prompt: 3 By 1700 A.D., the number of elements recognised was only:
blocks.explanation: By 1700 A.D. only 12 elements, such as gold, silver and copper, were recognised (1.1).

book_ref.quote: By 1700 A.D., only 12 elements

blocks.prompt: 4 Which one of the following was NOT among the 12 elements recognised by 1700 A.D.?
blocks.explanation: The twelve were gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, tin, mercury, phosphorus, sulfur, carbon, zinc and arsenic; sodium is not in the list (1.1).

book_ref.quote: Gold, Silver, Copper, Iron, Lead, Tin, Mercury, Phosphorus, Sulfur, Carbon, Zinc, and Arsenic

blocks.prompt: 5 Up to the end of the 18th century, Antoine Lavoisier tried to classify the known elements as:

options.text: s, p, d and f blocks

blocks.explanation: Lavoisier attempted to classify the known elements as metals and nonmetals (1.1).

book_ref.quote: Antoine Lavoisier attempted to classify known elements as metals and nonmetals

blocks.prompt: 6 Döbereiner grouped the elements into triads in the year:
blocks.explanation: In 1829 Döbereiner grouped elements into triads, groups of three with similar properties (1.1).

book_ref.quote: In 1829, Döbereiner grouped the elements into triads

blocks.prompt: 7 In a Döbereiner triad, the atomic weight of the middle element is:

options.text: the sum of the other two
twice that of the first element
roughly the average of the other two
half that of the third element

blocks.explanation: Döbereiner noted that the middle element's atomic weight was roughly the average of the other two (1.1).

book_ref.quote: noting that the atomic weight of the middle element was roughly the average of the other two

blocks.prompt: 8 Three elements with similar properties form a triad. The first and third have atomic masses 40 and 137. The triad rule predicts the atomic mass of the middle element to be about:

book_ref.quote: the middle one is the average of the other two, (7 + 39) ÷ 2 = 23

blocks.prompt: 9 John Newlands observed periodicity among how many known elements?
blocks.explanation: In 1864 Newlands observed periodicity in the 62 known elements (1.1).

book_ref.quote: first time observed periodicity in the 62 known elements

blocks.prompt: 10 When elements were arranged by increasing atomic masses, Newlands found that the first element resembled in properties:
blocks.explanation: Newlands grouped elements so that every eighth element resembled the first (1.1).

book_ref.quote: every eighth element resembled the first element in properties

blocks.prompt: 11 In 1869, Mendeleev arranged 63 elements in vertical columns in the order of increasing:
blocks.explanation: Mendeleev arranged 63 elements into eight vertical columns by increasing atomic mass (1.1).

book_ref.quote: arranged 63 elements into eight vertical columns by increasing atomic mass

blocks.prompt: 12 The success of Mendeleev's table was mainly due to:

options.text: leaving gaps for undiscovered elements and predicting their properties
placing elements in s, p, d and f blocks

blocks.explanation: He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their atomic masses and properties, which proved accurate (1.1).

book_ref.quote: The success of his table was hidden in leaving gaps for undiscovered elements

blocks.prompt: 13 Lothar Meyer's curves were obtained by plotting a graph between:
blocks.explanation: Lothar Meyer plotted atomic weights against atomic volumes; the curves showed periodicity (1.1).

book_ref.quote: plotting a graph between the atomic weights and atomic volumes of elements

blocks.prompt: 14 Moseley determined the exact atomic numbers of the known elements by using:
blocks.explanation: In 1913 Moseley found the exact atomic numbers using X-ray emission (1.1).

book_ref.quote: Moseley determined the exact atomic numbers of known elements using X-ray emission

blocks.prompt: 15 Moseley removed the flaws of Mendeleev's table by arranging the elements by:

options.text: atomic numbers instead of atomic masses
atomic masses instead of atomic numbers
atomic volumes instead of atomic masses

blocks.explanation: Moseley arranged elements by atomic numbers instead of atomic masses and modified the periodic law (1.1).

book_ref.quote: arranging the elements by atomic numbers instead of atomic masses

blocks.prompt: 16 Whose table was the first most notable effort in the classification of elements?
blocks.explanation: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic masses; his table was the first most notable classification (1.1).

book_ref.quote: his table was the first most notable effort in the classification of elements

blocks.text: 1.2 Modern periodic table: features and significance

blocks.prompt: 17 In the modern periodic table, the 118 elements are placed in ascending order of their:
blocks.explanation: Presently 118 elements are grouped in ascending order of atomic numbers (1.2).

book_ref.quote: grouped in the table in ascending order of their respective atomic numbers

blocks.prompt: 18 The number of horizontal rows (periods) in the modern periodic table is:
blocks.explanation: There are seven horizontal rows called periods (1.2).

book_ref.quote: There are seven horizontal rows called periods

blocks.prompt: 19 The number of vertical columns (groups) in the modern periodic table is:
blocks.explanation: The modern table has eighteen vertical columns called groups (1.2).

book_ref.quote: eighteen vertical columns called groups

blocks.prompt: 20 In older versions of the periodic table, the 8 vertical groups were divided into:
blocks.explanation: Older tables had 8 vertical groups divided into eight A-groups and ten B-groups (1.2).

book_ref.quote: Eight A-Groups and Ten B-Groups

blocks.prompt: 21 Elements of the same group show similar chemical properties because they have the same:
blocks.explanation: Elements of a group have the same number of valence electrons, so similar chemical properties (1.2).

book_ref.quote: because they have the same number of valence electrons

blocks.prompt: 22 From top to bottom in a group, the physical properties of elements:
blocks.explanation: Group members show a gradual change in physical properties from top to bottom (1.2).

book_ref.quote: they show a gradual change in physical properties from top to bottom in a group

blocks.prompt: 23 Metals are elements which tend to:

options.text: gain electrons to form negative ions
lose electrons to form positive ions

blocks.explanation: Metals tend to lose electrons and form positive ions, e.g. iron and copper (1.3).

book_ref.quote: Metals are elements which tend to lose electrons to form positive ions

blocks.prompt: 24 Which one of the following is a non-metal?
blocks.explanation: Non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions; examples are chlorine, sulfur and phosphorus (1.3).

book_ref.quote: The examples are chlorine, sulfur and phosphorous

blocks.prompt: 25 The "stair-step line" on the periodic table begins at:

options.text: hydrogen and extends down to francium
boron and extends down to polonium
carbon and extends down to lead
fluorine and extends down to astatine

blocks.explanation: The stair-step line begins at boron and extends down to polonium (1.3).

book_ref.quote: The line begins at boron (B) and extends down to polonium (Po)

blocks.prompt: 26 Which one of the following is a metalloid?
blocks.explanation: Elements along the stair-step line such as Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te are metalloids (1.3).

book_ref.quote: including Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te

blocks.prompt: 27 Elements that show properties of both metals and nonmetals are also termed:
blocks.explanation: Elements just to the right of the line are metalloids or semimetals (1.3).

book_ref.quote: are termed as metalloids or semimetals

blocks.prompt: 28 Which element is the exception to the rule that elements to the left of the stair-step line are metals?
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen, the first element, is the exception (1.3).

book_ref.quote: The exception is hydrogen, the first element on the periodic table

blocks.prompt: 29 Elements are classified into blocks on the basis of:

options.text: the subshell containing their valence electrons

blocks.explanation: Blocks are based on the subshell that holds the valence electrons (1.4).

book_ref.quote: based on the subshells containing their valence electrons

blocks.prompt: 30 The elements of the first two groups belong to the:
blocks.explanation: Their valence electrons are in s subshells, placing them in the s-block (1.4).

book_ref.quote: placing these elements in the s-block

blocks.prompt: 31 Transition elements belong to the:
blocks.explanation: Transition elements belong to the d-block (1.4).

book_ref.quote: transition elements belong to the d-block

blocks.prompt: 32 The lanthanides and actinides, the two series at the bottom of the table, are:
blocks.explanation: Lanthanides and actinides are categorised as f-block elements (1.4).

book_ref.quote: are categorized as f-block elements

blocks.prompt: 33 The elements of groups 13 to 18, including the gases of the last group, belong to the:
blocks.explanation: The remaining elements in groups 13 to 18 belong to the p-block (1.4).

book_ref.quote: including the inert gases in the last group, belong to the p-block

blocks.prompt: 34 An element family is:

options.text: a single horizontal row of elements
elements having the same atomic mass
a set of elements sharing common properties

blocks.explanation: An element family is a set of elements sharing common properties (1.5).

book_ref.quote: An element family is a set of elements sharing common properties

blocks.prompt: 35 Group 1 elements are called alkali metals because they:

options.text: are found mostly in the earth
produce alkalis when they react with water

blocks.explanation: Group 1 elements produce alkalis on reaction with water, hence alkali metals (u-i).

book_ref.quote: because they produce alkalis when they react with water

blocks.prompt: 36 Which one of the following is NOT a property of alkali metals?
blocks.explanation: Alkali metals have one valence electron, low densities, relatively low melting points and low ionization energies (1.5).

book_ref.quote: Alkali metals are characterized by one valence electron, low densities

blocks.prompt: 37 Alkaline earth metals are divalent because they have:

options.text: a valency equal to their period number
two electrons in their valence shell

blocks.explanation: Group 2 elements have two valence electrons, making them divalent (1.5).

book_ref.quote: These elements have two electrons in their valence shell, making them divalent

blocks.prompt: 38 Compared with alkali metals, alkaline earth metals are:
blocks.explanation: Alkaline earth metals are metallic solids harder and denser than alkali metals (1.5).

book_ref.quote: harder and denser than alkali metals

blocks.prompt: 39 The largest family of elements in the middle of the periodic table is the:
blocks.explanation: The transition metals make up the largest family in the middle of the table (1.5).

book_ref.quote: The transition metals make up the largest family of elements

blocks.prompt: 40 Which property is typical of transition elements?
blocks.explanation: Transition elements have high melting points, high density and variable oxidation states, and mostly form coloured compounds (1.5).

book_ref.quote: high melting points, high density, and variable oxidation states

blocks.prompt: 41 Group 16 elements are called chalcogens because:

options.text: most ores of copper (Greek chalkos) are oxides or sulfides
they form salts with alkali metals
they are found free in air

blocks.explanation: Chalcogens are named from copper (chalkos) ores, most of which are oxides or sulfides (1.5).

book_ref.quote: because most ores of copper (Greek chalkos) are oxides or sulfides

blocks.prompt: 42 In group 16, the non-metals are:
blocks.explanation: In group 16, oxygen and sulphur are non-metals (1.5).

book_ref.quote: oxygen & sulphur are non-metals

blocks.prompt: 43 The element at the bottom of group 16 is:
blocks.explanation: Element 116, livermorium, is at the bottom of group 16 and is a metal (1.5).

book_ref.quote: is a misprint for livermorium (Lv, element 116)

blocks.prompt: 44 The term "halogen" means:
blocks.explanation: Halogens easily react with alkali and alkaline earth metals to form stable halide salts; halogen means "salt-former" (1.5).

book_ref.quote: these elements easily react with alkali metals and alkaline earth metals to form stable halide salts

blocks.prompt: 45 Halogens complete their outermost shell by:
blocks.explanation: Halogens easily accept one electron to complete their outermost shell (1.5).

book_ref.quote: Halogens can easily accept one electron to complete their outermost shell

blocks.prompt: 46 Halogens are highly reactive nonmetals having:
blocks.explanation: Halogens are highly reactive nonmetals with high electron affinities (1.5).

book_ref.quote: Halogens are highly reactive nonmetals with high electron affinities

blocks.prompt: 47 Noble gases exist in nature as:
blocks.explanation: Noble gases are monoatomic in nature (1.5).

book_ref.quote: These elements are monoatomic in nature

blocks.prompt: 48 Which compound shows that noble gases are not completely unreactive?
blocks.explanation: Xenon forms compounds such as xenon hexafluoroplatinate, XePtF₆; so "inert gases" were renamed "noble gases" (1.5).

book_ref.quote: xenon hexafluoroplatinate (XePtF₆)

blocks.prompt: 49 Noble gases are almost entirely unreactive under normal conditions because they have:
blocks.explanation: Their stable configuration with a complete outermost shell makes them almost unreactive (1.5).

book_ref.quote: Due to their stable electron configuration (complete outermost shell)

blocks.prompt: 50 Which element belongs to the halogen family?
blocks.explanation: The halogens listed are F, Cl, Br, I, At and Ts (1.5).

book_ref.quote: Halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At, Ts)

blocks.prompt: 51 Which one of the following is a noble gas?
blocks.explanation: The noble gases are He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn and Og (1.5).

book_ref.quote: Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, Og)

blocks.prompt: 52 Which element belongs to the alkaline earth metals?
blocks.explanation: The alkaline earth family is Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra (1.5, book correction).

book_ref.quote: The family is Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra

blocks.prompt: 53 Which one of the following is listed among the transition metals?
blocks.explanation: The transition metals listed are Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu and Zn (1.5).

book_ref.quote: Transition metals (Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn)

blocks.prompt: 54 The period number of an element indicates:

options.text: the number of electron shells (principal quantum number n)

blocks.explanation: The period number gives n, the number of electron shells around the nucleus (1.6).

book_ref.quote: The period number indicates the principal quantum number (n)

blocks.prompt: 55 The subshell in which the valence electrons of an element are found depends on the element's:
blocks.explanation: The subshell of the valence electrons depends on the element's block (azimuthal quantum number) (1.6).

book_ref.quote: The specific subshell where the valence electrons are found

blocks.prompt: 56 An element is in period 3, group 1 (s-block). Its electronic configuration is:
blocks.explanation: Period 3 means three shells; group 1 in the s-block means one valence electron in 3s: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ (1.6).

book_ref.quote: an element X in the 3rd period has three electron shells

blocks.prompt: 57 An element has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹. Its position in the periodic table is:
blocks.explanation: Three shells give period 3; three valence electrons in 3s² 3p¹ give group 13 (1.6).

book_ref.quote: the element X belongs to group 13 of periodic table so it has 3 valence electrons

blocks.prompt: 58 For an s-block element in group 2, the group number tells us that it has:
blocks.explanation: The group number indicates the number of valence electrons; group 2 means two in the outermost shell (1.6).

book_ref.quote: the group number indicates the number of valence electrons

blocks.prompt: 59 According to the Modern Periodic Law, the properties of elements are periodic functions of their:
blocks.explanation: The Modern Periodic Law: physical and chemical properties are periodic functions of atomic numbers (1.7).

book_ref.quote: The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

blocks.prompt: 60 The atomic number of an element corresponds to the number of:
blocks.explanation: The atomic number corresponds to the number of protons in an atom (1.7).

book_ref.quote: The atomic number corresponds to the number of protons in an atom

blocks.prompt: 61 When elements are arranged by increasing atomic number, which element shows many properties similar to lithium?
blocks.explanation: Sodium, potassium and cesium are in the same group as lithium and show similar properties (1.7).

book_ref.quote: sodium, potassium, and cesium exhibit many physical and chemical characteristics similar to lithium

blocks.prompt: 62 The atomic radius is:

options.text: half of the distance between two identical atoms bonded together
the full distance between two identical bonded atoms
the radius of the nucleus only
twice the distance between two bonded atoms

blocks.explanation: Atomic radius is half the distance between two identical atoms bonded together (1.7.1).

book_ref.quote: It is half of the distance between two identical atoms bonded together

blocks.prompt: 63 The distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together is 228 pm. The atomic radius is:
blocks.explanation: Atomic radius = half the distance = 228 ÷ 2 = 114 pm (1.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The atomic radius is a measure of the size of an atom

blocks.prompt: 64 Atomic radius is typically measured in:
blocks.explanation: Atomic radius is typically measured in picometres (pm) or angstroms (Å) (1.7.1).

book_ref.quote: typically measured in picometers (pm) or Angstroms (Å)

blocks.prompt: 65 The atomic radius of an element can vary depending upon:

options.text: the type of bond (covalent, metallic, van der Waals)

blocks.explanation: Atomic radius can vary with the type of bond (covalent, metallic, van der Waals) or the state of the atom (1.7.1).

book_ref.quote: depending on the type of bond (covalent, metallic & van der Waals forces)

blocks.prompt: 66 Which one of the following is NOT listed as a factor affecting atomic radius?
blocks.explanation: The factors are atomic number, effective nuclear charge and shielding effect of inner electrons (1.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The factors affecting the atomic radius are: atomic number, effective nuclear charge and shielding effect of inner electrons

blocks.prompt: 67 Atomic radius increases down a group mainly because:
blocks.explanation: Down a group extra shells are added; more shielding outweighs the higher nuclear charge (1.7.1).

book_ref.quote: because additional electron shells are added

blocks.prompt: 68 Atomic radius decreases across a period from left to right because:

options.text: increasing nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud closer

blocks.explanation: Across a period the increasing nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud closer (1.7.1).

book_ref.quote: due to increasing nuclear charge, which pulls the electron cloud closer

blocks.prompt: 69 The ionic radius is a measure of the size of:

options.text: a neutral atom in a gas
an ion in a crystal lattice

blocks.explanation: The ionic radius measures the size of an ion in a crystal lattice (1.7.2).

book_ref.quote: The ionic radius is a measure of the size of an ion in a crystal lattice

blocks.prompt: 70 A positive ion is smaller than its neutral atom because the loss of electrons:

options.text: reduces electronic repulsion so the remaining electrons are pulled closer

blocks.explanation: Losing electrons reduces repulsion; the remaining electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus (1.7.2).

book_ref.quote: the loss of electrons reduces electronic repulsion

blocks.prompt: 71 When an atom gains electrons to form an anion, it becomes larger because:

options.text: electronic repulsion increases and the electron cloud expands

blocks.explanation: Added electrons increase repulsion; the nuclear pull on each electron decreases and the cloud expands (1.7.2).

book_ref.quote: the addition of electrons increases electronic repulsion

blocks.prompt: 72 Which statement about sizes is correct?

options.text: Cl⁻ is larger than the Cl atom
Na⁺ is larger than the Na atom
Cl⁻ and the Cl atom are the same size
Na⁺ and the Na atom are the same size

blocks.explanation: An anion is larger and a cation smaller than the neutral atom, so Cl⁻ is larger than Cl (1.7.2).

book_ref.quote: it generally becomes larger than the neutral atom

blocks.prompt: 73 Across a period from left to right, the ionic radius of anions:
blocks.explanation: The increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer, so anion radius also decreases across a period (1.7.2).

book_ref.quote: For anions, the ionic radius also decreases across a period

blocks.prompt: 74 Cations and anions increase in size down a group because:

options.text: the principal quantum number n and the number of shells increase

blocks.explanation: Down a group n increases, adding shells; this outweighs the higher nuclear charge (1.7.2).

book_ref.quote: both cations and anions increase in size as we move down a group

blocks.prompt: 75 The first ionization energy refers to the removal of an electron from atoms of an element in the:
blocks.explanation: 1st ionization energy is for one mole of atoms in the gaseous state forming gaseous 1+ ions (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: in one mole of atoms of the element in the gaseous state

blocks.prompt: 76 The second ionization energy of calcium given in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: Ca⁺(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + e⁻, ΔHᵢ₂ = 1150 kJ mol⁻¹ (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: If a second electron is removed from each ion in a mole of gaseous 1+ ions

blocks.prompt: 77 Using ΔHᵢ₁ = 590 and ΔHᵢ₂ = 1150 kJ mol⁻¹, the total energy to change 1 mol of Ca(g) into Ca²⁺(g) is:
blocks.explanation: Both electrons are removed: 590 + 1150 = 1740 kJ (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: we call it the 2nd ionization energy

blocks.prompt: 78 Using ΔHᵢ₁ = 590, ΔHᵢ₂ = 1150 and ΔHᵢ₃ = 4940 kJ mol⁻¹, the energy needed to change 0.5 mol of Ca(g) into Ca³⁺(g) is:

book_ref.quote: Removal of a third electron from each ion in a mole of gaseous 2+ ions corresponds to the 3rd ionization energy

blocks.prompt: 79 How many ionization energies can an atom of magnesium (atomic number 12) have?
blocks.explanation: An element can have as many ionization energies as its atomic number, so magnesium has 12 (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: the exact number corresponds to its atomic number

blocks.prompt: 80 The first ionization energy of sodium is 494 kJ mol⁻¹. The energy needed to ionize 0.25 mol of Na(g) atoms to Na⁺(g) is:

book_ref.quote: to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions is known as 1st ionization energy

blocks.prompt: 81 Greater the effective nuclear charge of an atom:
blocks.explanation: A greater effective nuclear charge attracts the electron more, so ionization energy increases (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: ionisation energy increases with an increase in the effective nuclear charge

blocks.prompt: 82 As the size of an atom increases, its ionization energy:
blocks.explanation: In bigger atoms the nucleus attracts the outermost electrons weakly, so ionization energy decreases (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: the ionization energy decreases as the size of the atom increases

blocks.prompt: 83 Noble gases have the highest ionization energies in their periods because of their:
blocks.explanation: Their fully-filled ns² np⁶ shells are highly stable (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: Noble gases have highest ionisation energies in their respective periods

blocks.prompt: 84 Oxygen has a lower first ionization energy than nitrogen because:

options.text: oxygen has a smaller nuclear charge
nitrogen's half-filled 2p sub-shell is extra stable
oxygen has fewer shells than nitrogen

blocks.explanation: Although N has one unit less nuclear charge, its half-filled sub-shell is extra stable; O also has a spin-paired 2p electron (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: due to the extra-stability of the half-filled sub-shell of nitrogen

blocks.prompt: 85 The first ionization energies of nitrogen and oxygen are 1403 and 1314 kJ mol⁻¹. How much less is the value for oxygen?

book_ref.quote: The first ionization energy of oxygen is about 1314 kJ mol⁻¹, not 1365

blocks.prompt: 86 A larger number of inner electrons in an atom results in:

options.text: less screening and higher ionization energy
greater screening and higher ionization energy
greater screening and lower ionization energy

blocks.explanation: More inner electrons mean greater screening, so the ionization energy is lower (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: Larger the number of inner electrons, greater is the screening effect

blocks.prompt: 87 Spin-pair repulsion makes the removal of an electron from a spin-paired orbital:
blocks.explanation: Paired electrons repel each other, making it slightly easier to remove one of them (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: making it slightly easier to remove one of the paired electrons

blocks.prompt: 88 The correct order of first ionization energies in group 1 is:
blocks.explanation: Down group 1, size and shielding increase, so IE decreases: Li > Na > K > Rb > Cs (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: In Group I, the ionization energies decrease in the following order

blocks.prompt: 89 The valence electron of Cs is easier to remove than that of Rb because it is:

options.text: a 5s electron closer to the nucleus
a 6s electron farther from the nucleus
attracted by a smaller nuclear charge

blocks.explanation: The 6s electron of Cs is farther from the nucleus than the 5s electron of Rb (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: the 6s valence electron of Cs is farther from the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 90 Across a period from left to right:

options.text: a new shell is added for each element
the number of shells stays the same and effective nuclear charge increases
the shielding by the same shell increases sharply

blocks.explanation: Across a period the shells stay the same and effective nuclear charge rises, so IE increases (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: no. of shells remains unchanged while the effective nuclear charge increases

blocks.prompt: 91 In each period, the lowest ionization energy is shown by the:
blocks.explanation: Figure 1.6 shows alkali metals with the lowest and noble gases with the highest ionization energies (1.7.3).

book_ref.quote: whereas alkali metals have lowest values of ionization energy

blocks.prompt: 92 The first electron affinity is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form:
blocks.explanation: First EA forms 1 mole of gaseous uni-negative ions under standard conditions (1.7.4).

book_ref.quote: to form 1 mole of gaseous uni-negative ions under standard conditions

blocks.prompt: 93 The first electron affinity of chlorine (−348.8 kJ mol⁻¹) carries a negative sign because:
blocks.explanation: Energy is released when Cl(g) gains an electron, so the first EA is negative (1.7.4).

book_ref.quote: Since, energy is released, so first electron affinity carries negative sign

blocks.prompt: 94 The second electron affinity of oxygen, O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g), is:
blocks.explanation: 798 kJ mol⁻¹ is absorbed on adding the second electron to O⁻, so ΔH°ₑₐ₂ = +798 kJ mol⁻¹ (1.7.4).

book_ref.quote: But 798 kJ mol⁻¹ of energy is absorbed on adding second electron

blocks.prompt: 95 Using ΔH°ₑₐ₁ = −141 and ΔH°ₑₐ₂ = +798 kJ mol⁻¹, the net enthalpy change for forming 2 mol of O²⁻(g) from O(g) is:

book_ref.quote: The net enthalpy change for the formation of the oxide ion (O²⁻) can be calculated

blocks.prompt: 96 The first electron affinity of chlorine is −348.8 kJ mol⁻¹. The energy released when 0.5 mol of Cl(g) atoms form Cl⁻(g) is:
blocks.explanation: Energy released = 0.5 × 348.8 = 174.4 kJ (1.7.4).

book_ref.quote: This is amount of energy released when 6.02 × 10²³ atoms of chlorine

blocks.prompt: 97 Smaller the size of an atom:
blocks.explanation: In small atoms the nucleus attracts the incoming electron strongly, so EA is greater (1.7.4).

book_ref.quote: smaller is the size of the atom, greater is its electron affinity

blocks.prompt: 98 With an increase in the magnitude of nuclear charge, electron affinity:
blocks.explanation: A greater nuclear charge attracts the incoming electron more strongly, so EA increases (1.7.4).

book_ref.quote: with the increase in the magnitude of nuclear charge, electron affinity also increases

blocks.prompt: 99 The electron affinities of N and P are very low because they have:
blocks.explanation: N (2s² 2p³) and P (3s² 3p³) have stable half-filled p-subshells with little tendency to accept an electron (1.7.4).

book_ref.quote: These half-filled p-subshells, being very stable, have very little tendency to accept any extra electron

blocks.prompt: 100 Noble gas atoms do not accept an extra electron. This is shown by their:
blocks.explanation: With stable ns² np⁶ configuration, noble gases have positive 1st electron affinities (1.7.4).

book_ref.quote: This is evident from their positive 1st electron affinities

blocks.prompt: 101 Among the halogens, the most negative electron affinity is shown by:
blocks.explanation: The order is At < I < Br < F < Cl; chlorine (−349.0 kJ/mol) is the most negative (1.7.5).

book_ref.quote: This trend is observed in the halogens (At < I < Br < F < Cl)

blocks.prompt: 102 From Table 1.1, Li has electron affinity −60.0 and Cs −46.0 kJ/mol. How much more energy is released per mole by Li?
